'''Louis Eugene Brus'''<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 13, 2023 |title=Louis Eugene Brus |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/louis-eugene-brus |access-date=October 4, 2023 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref> (August 10, 1943 – January 11, 2026) was an American chemist, and the Samuel Latham Mitchell Professor of [[Chemistry]] at [[Columbia University]]. He was the co-discoverer of the [[colloid]]al [[semi-conductor]] nanocrystals known as [[quantum dots]].<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://scitation.aip.org/content/aip/journal/jcp/80/9/10.1063/1.447218 |first=Louis E.| last=Brus|title=Electron–electron and electron-hole interactions in small semiconductor crystallites: The size dependence of the lowest excited electronic state |year=1984 |journal=[[The Journal of Chemical Physics]] |accessdate=January 30, 2015| volume=80| issue=4403|pages=4403–4409|doi=10.1063/1.447218|bibcode=1984JChPh..80.4403B|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In 2023, he was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]].

==Early life and education==
Louis Eugene Brus was born in [[Cleveland]], Ohio, on August 10, 1943.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7g1LAQAAIAAJ&q=Louis+Eugene+Brus+Aug.+10+,+1943|title=Who's Who in Science and Engineering 2008-2009|first1=Who's Who|last1=Marquis|first2=Marquis Who's|last2=Who|date=December 18, 2007|publisher=Marquis Who's Who|isbn=978-0-8379-5768-5 |via=Google Books}}</ref> During high school in [[Roeland Park, Kansas]], he developed an interest in chemistry and [[physics]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Davis |first=Tinsley |date=February 2005 |title=Biography of Louis E. Brus |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=102 |issue=5 |pages=1277–1279 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0409555102 |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=547879 |pmid=15677326 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

He entered [[Rice University]] in 1961 with a [[Naval Reserve Officers Training Corps]] (NROTC) college scholarship, which required him to participate in NROTC activities at sea as a [[midshipman]]. In 1965, he graduated from Rice with a [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] degree in chemical physics, and then moved to [[Columbia University]] for his doctoral research.<ref name=":1" /> For his [[Thesis|dissertation]], he worked on the [[photodissociation]] of [[sodium iodide]] vapor, under the supervision of [[Richard Bersohn]].<ref name=":1" /> After obtaining his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] degree in chemical physics in 1969, Brus returned to the Navy as a lieutenant and served as a scientific staff officer in collaboration with [[Lin Ming-chang]], at the [[United States Naval Research Laboratory]] in [[Washington, D.C.]]<ref name=":1" />

Under the recommendation of Bersohn, Brus left the Navy permanently and joined [[Bell Labs|AT&T Bell Laboratories]] in 1973, where he did the work that led to the discovery of [[Quantum dot|quantum dots]].<ref name=":1" /> In 1996, Brus left Bell Labs and joined the faculty in the Department of Chemistry at [[Columbia University]].<ref name=":1" />

==Work on quantum dots==
Brus was a foundational figure in the research and development of [[Quantum dot|quantum dots]]. Quantum dots are tiny semiconducting crystals whose nanoscale size gives them unique optical and electronic properties.<ref name="Singh">{{cite journal |last1=Singh |first1=Suchita |last2=Dhawan |first2=Aksha |last3=Karhana |first3=Sonali |last4=Bhat |first4=Madhusudan |last5=Dinda |first5=Amit Kumar |title=Quantum Dots: An Emerging Tool for Point-of-Care Testing |journal=Micromachines |date=November 29, 2020 |volume=11 |issue=12 |pages=1058 |doi=10.3390/mi11121058 |pmid=33260478 |pmc=7761335 |issn=2072-666X |doi-access=free }}</ref> He was independently the first to synthesize them in a solution in 1982. At the time, he was studying [[organic photochemistry]] on [[cadmium sulfide]] particle surfaces using pump–probe [[Raman spectroscopy]], looking for possible applications for solar-energy.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=Robinson |first=Julia |title=The quantum dot story |url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/the-quantum-dot-story/4018219.article |access-date=October 20, 2023 |website=Chemistry World |language=en}}</ref> He noticed that the optical properties of the crystals changed after leaving them for 24 hours.<ref name=":3" /> He attributed this change in [[band gap]] energy to [[Ostwald ripening]] when the crystal increased in size.<ref name=":3" /> Brus provided the theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of quantum dots in terms of quantum size effects. He identified the connection between the particle size of semiconductors and the wavelength of the light they emit,<ref name="Sanderson">{{cite journal |last1=Sanderson |first1=Katharine |last2=Castelvecchi |first2=Davide |title=Tiny 'quantum dot' particles win chemistry Nobel |journal=Nature |date=October 4, 2023 |volume=622 |issue=7982 |pages=227–228 |doi=10.1038/d41586-023-03048-9 |pmid=37794149 |bibcode=2023Natur.622..227S |s2cid=263671129 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-03048-9 |language=en|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Efros">{{cite journal |last1=Efros |first1=Alexander L. |last2=Brus |first2=Louis E. |title=Nanocrystal Quantum Dots: From Discovery to Modern Development |journal=ACS Nano |date=April 27, 2021 |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=6192–6210 |doi=10.1021/acsnano.1c01399 |pmid=33830732 |bibcode=2021ACSNa..15.6192E |s2cid=233193323 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acsnano.1c01399 |language=en |issn=1936-0851|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Bubola">{{cite news |last1=Bubola |first1=Emma |last2=Miller |first2=Katrina |title=Nobel Prize in Chemistry Awarded to 3 Scientists for Exploring the Nanoworld |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/10/04/science/nobel-prize-chemistry.html |work=The New York Times |date=October 4, 2023}}</ref><ref name="Gramling">{{cite news |last1=Gramling |first1=Carolyn |title=The development of quantum dots wins the 2023 Nobel prize in chemistry |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/quantum-dots-nanoparticles-bawendi-brus-ekimov |work=Science News |date=October 4, 2023}}</ref><ref name="Clery">{{cite news |last1=Clery |first1=Daniel |last2=Kean |first2=Sam |title=Creators of quantum dots, used in TV displays and cell studies, win chemistry Nobel |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/creators-of-quantum-dots-used-in-tv-displays-and-cell-studies-win-chemistry-nobel |work=Science |date=October 4, 2023}}</ref> now known as the [[Brus equation]].<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Kafel |first1=A. |last2=Al-Rashid |first2=S. N. Turki |title=Study Using the Brus Equation to Examine How Quantum Confinement Energy Affects the Optical Characteristics of Cadmium Sulfide and Zinc Selenide |journal=International Journal of Nanoscience |date=January 1, 2023 |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=2350034–120 |doi=10.1142/S0219581X23500345 |bibcode=2023IJN....2250034K |s2cid=258431435 |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023IJN....2250034K/abstract |issn=0219-581X}}</ref>

Brus tried to contact researchers in the Soviet Union. It was in 1990 that he finally met [[Alexey Ekimov]] and [[Alexander Efros]], who had first developed the semiconductor nanocrystals in glass in 1981 under more rudimentary conditions, however their research was not available in the United States.<ref name=":3" />

At Bell Labs, Brus worked with postdoc researchers [[Paul Alivisatos]] and [[Moungi Bawendi]] in a research project with organometallic synthetic chemist Michael L. Steigerwald on reducing the size of the quantum dots.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dukovic |first=Gordana |date=2026-04-16 |title=Louis E. Brus (1943–2026) |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41565-026-02157-6 |journal=Nature Nanotechnology |language=en |doi=10.1038/s41565-026-02157-6 |issn=1748-3387|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite Q|Q140845501}}</ref>

==Death==
Brus died of [[myelodysplastic syndrome]] in [[Hastings-on-Hudson, New York]] on January 11, 2026, at the age of 82.<ref>{{cite web|title=Louis E. Brus, Nobel Laureate Who Illuminated the Nanoworld, Dies at 82|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/23/science/louis-e-brus-dead.html|last=Miller|first=Katrina|publisher=The New York Times|date=January 23, 2025|access-date=January 25, 2025}}</ref><ref> {{cite web |title= Brus, Rice alumnus and Nobel laureate, passes away at 82 |url= https://news.rice.edu/news/2026/brus-rice-alumnus-and-nobel-laureate-passes-away-82 |website=Rice University |access-date=January 13, 2026}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Brus was elected a [[fellow]] of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1998,<ref>{{cite news |date=May 28, 1998 |title=Curl Elected AAAS Fellow |publisher=Rice University |url=https://news2.rice.edu/1998/05/28/curl-elected-aaas-fellow/ |access-date=July 18, 2023}}</ref> a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 2004,<ref>{{cite news |title=Louis E. Brus |publisher=National Academy of Sciences |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/louis-e-brus-oxtges/ |access-date=July 18, 2023}}</ref> and was a member of the [[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Gruppe 4: Kjemi |url=http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40122 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120303133407/http://www.dnva.no/c26849/artikkel/vis.html?tid=40122 |archive-date=March 3, 2012 |accessdate=October 7, 2010 |publisher=[[Norwegian Academy of Science and Letters]] |language=Norwegian}}</ref>

He received the Distinguished Alumni Award from the Association of [[Rice University]] Alumni in 2010. He was co-recipient of the 2006 [[R. W. Wood Prize]] of the [[Optical Society of America]] "for the discovery of nanocrystal quantum dots and pioneering studies of their electronic and optical properties" shared with Alexander Efros and Alexey Ekimov.<ref>{{cite web |title=R. W. Wood Prize |url=https://www.optica.org/get_involved/awards_and_honors/awards/award_descriptions/rwwood/ |website=Optica}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=August 30, 2006 |title=Twenty attain 2006 top honors from the OSA |url=https://www.laserfocusworld.com/test-measurement/research/article/16567206/twenty-attain-2006-top-honors-from-the-osa |access-date=October 4, 2023 |website=Laser Focus World}}</ref> He also received the inaugural [[Kavli Prize]] for [[nanoscience]] along with [[Sumio Iijima]] in 2008 for "their large impact in the development of the nanoscience field of the zero and one dimensional nanostructures in physics, chemistry and [[biology]]".<ref>{{cite news |year=2008 |title=Columbia Professors to Receive Kavli Prizes in Norway Ceremony |url=http://www.columbia.edu/cu/news/research/kavli.html |accessdate=June 25, 2010}}</ref> In 2009 he was awarded the [[Willard Gibbs Award]] "for his leading role in the creation of chemical quantum dots".<ref>{{cite web|title=Gibbs Award Ceremony 2009|url=http://archive.chicagoacs.net/meetings/09may.html|website=Chicago ACS Archive|publisher=Chicago Section of the American Chemical Society|access-date=February 10, 2016}}</ref> Brus was chosen for the 2010 [[NAS Award in Chemical Sciences]]. In 2012 he received the [[Franklin Institute]]'s [[Bower Award and Prize for Achievement in Science]],<ref>{{cite web |year=2012 |title=Bower Award and Prize for Achievement in Science |url=http://www.fi.edu/franklinawards/12/bowersci.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121217010823/http://www.fi.edu/franklinawards/12/bowersci.html |archive-date=December 17, 2012 |accessdate=April 7, 2013 |publisher=[[Franklin Institute]]}}</ref> and was selected as a [[List of Clarivate Citation laureates in Chemistry|Clarivate Citation laureate in Chemistry]] "for discovery of colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals (quantum dots)".<ref>{{Cite press release |publisher=Thomson Reuters |title=Thomson Reuters Predicts 2012 Nobel Laureates |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/thomson-reuters-predicts-2012-nobel-laureates-170285846.html |access-date=October 4, 2023 |website=www.prnewswire.com |language=en}}</ref> 

In 2023, Brus was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] jointly with Ekimov and Moungi Bawendi "for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots".<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last1=Devlin |first1=Hannah |date=October 4, 2023 |title=Scientists share Nobel prize in chemistry for quantum dots discovery |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2023/oct/04/nobel-prize-in-chemistry-winners-2023 |access-date=October 4, 2023 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Bawendi had worked as a postdoc with Brus, when they were in Bell Labs.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 4, 2023 |title=Names of purported Nobel chemistry prize winners inadvertently released |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/names-purported-nobel-chemistry-prize-winners-inadvertently-released-2023-10-04/ |access-date=October 4, 2023}}</ref>

He was inducted as a 2025 fellow of the [[National Academy of Inventors]].<ref>{{cite web |year=2025 |title=National Academy of Inventors Fellows Class of 2025 |url=https://academyofinventors.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/2025-Fellows-List.pdf |accessdate=January 7, 2025}}</ref>
